01_bluetooth-flight-diversion.json.script: A United Airlines flight bound for Spain turned around mid-Atlantic and flew back to New Jersey. The reason: a passenger's phone Bluetooth network was named something that scared the crew. The plane had already been airborne for hours when the captain made the call. 264 passengers got grounded. United said the threat wasn't real, just a name. The FAA is now looking at whether new rules are needed. One Wi-Fi nickname cost an airline tens of thousands of dollars.

01_las-vegas-blanket-fort.json.title: High Schoolers Just Built a Blanket Fort So Big It Beat a World Record
01_las-vegas-blanket-fort.json.script: High school students in Las Vegas just built a blanket fort so massive it officially broke a Guinness World Record. The fort stretched across 14,103 square feet at a local community center — larger than most houses. Students from West Career and Technical Academy designed it all, using donated sheets and scaffolding. Guinness rules: no gaps bigger than 1 inch, sheets must touch the floor, and people must be able to sit inside. Previous record: 12,291 square feet. Gone.

02_tasmanian-devil-escape.json.title: An Endangered Tasmanian Devil Escaped a Wildlife Park. Nobody Can Find Her.
02_tasmanian-devil-escape.json.script: A 2-year-old Tasmanian devil named Mary escaped from a wildlife park in Queensland, Australia — and has been on the run for 4 days. She's endangered, nocturnal, and can roam 10 miles in a single night. Twelve wildlife experts, thermal imaging drones, and a sniffer dog have searched around the clock. CCTV shows Mary sprinting into the dark just hours before anyone noticed. Tasmanian devils have been extinct on the Australian mainland for 3,000 years. Nobody's found her yet.

03_bayville-blank-ballot.json.script: The village of Bayville on Long Island has 7,000 residents and a mayoral election on June 16. There is just one problem: nobody ran. The sitting mayor stepped down. No one else filed by the deadline. Officials say this has never happened before in Bayville's history. 05_nasa-x59-sonic-boom.json.title: NASA's Sonic Boom Killer Just Broke the Sound Barrier for the First Time
05_nasa-x59-sonic-boom.json.script: NASA's experimental X-59 jet crossed Mach 1 for the first time on June 5, 2026. The plane hit Mach 1.1 at 43,000 feet above the California desert. The X-59 is NASA's answer to the Concorde problem: it flies supersonic but generates a quiet thump instead of a boom. If regulators approve, overland supersonic flights could return for the first time in 50 years. Concorde retired in 2003 because the sonic boom was too loud. That excuse just ran out.
